content.overview: Cultivation genetics is the study of inherited variation and how that variation is expressed under real developmental and environmental conditions. Breeding decisions become defensible when genotype, phenotype, pedigree, population size, segregation, recombination, environment, selection criteria, replication and progeny performance are documented separately instead of collapsing every observed trait into a simple genetic claim.

vocabulary.definition: The genetic constitution of an organism at one or more loci or across its genome.
The observable characteristics produced by the interaction of genotype, development and environment.
A condition in which different genotypes respond differently to environmental conditions, changing their relative phenotypic performance.
Separation of alleles during reproduction that creates different genetic combinations among offspring.
Formation of new combinations of inherited genetic material during meiosis and reproduction.
Choosing which individuals contribute disproportionately to a later generation based on defined breeding goals.

sections.title: Phenotype is evidence, not a complete genetic explanation
sections.body: An observed trait reflects inherited potential interacting with developmental stage and environment. One plant expressing a desirable phenotype does not prove the trait is genetically fixed, highly heritable, or likely to transmit unchanged to its offspring.

sections.title: Related plants can still differ substantially
sections.body: Sexual reproduction produces new combinations of parental alleles through segregation and recombination. Siblings can therefore differ in morphology, vigor, flowering behavior, chemistry and stress response without any labeling error being involved.

sections.title: Environment can change expression and ranking
sections.body: The same genotype can express differently under different conditions, and different genotypes may not respond to an environmental change in the same way. When possible, record relevant environment and repeat evaluation before treating one ranking as universal.

sections.title: Pedigree is a hypothesis about inheritance, not proof of phenotype
sections.body: Parentage records describe ancestry and mating history. They do not guarantee that every offspring will display a named parental trait or that a complex trait follows a simple one-gene pattern.

sections.title: Simple Mendelian examples are useful but limited
sections.body: Dominant and recessive models help explain allele segregation at individual loci, but many cultivation traits are influenced by multiple loci, development and environment. Avoid forcing complex traits into unsupported single-gene explanations.

sections.title: Population size affects what the breeder can observe
sections.body: A small family samples only part of the possible genetic variation. Rare combinations may be missed entirely, so conclusions about uniformity, absence of a trait, or selection response should include the number of individuals actually evaluated.

sections.title: Selection changes allele and trait representation
sections.body: Choosing parents changes which genetic combinations contribute to the next generation. Selection should use predefined traits, consistent measurement and records of both selected and rejected individuals so decisions remain auditable.

sections.title: Progeny evidence strengthens genetic claims
sections.body: If a parent repeatedly produces offspring with a desired trait under documented conditions, the evidence for useful transmission becomes stronger. One exceptional parent phenotype without progeny evidence is much weaker evidence of breeding value.

sections.title: Stability requires repeated evidence
sections.body: Terms such as stable, uniform or fixed should be tied to observations across relevant generations, families and conditions. A single generation or a few selected plants cannot establish broad stability by itself.

workedExamples: Two siblings from one cross differ sharply in aroma and plant architecture. The variation is consistent with segregation, recombination and environmental interaction; it does not by itself indicate a labeling mistake.
A candidate performs best only in the highest-light position. Repeat or balanced evaluation is needed before treating that plant as genetically superior for vigor.

A recessive single-locus teaching example predicts a ratio, but a small family does not match that ratio closely. Sampling variation is a plausible explanation before assuming the inheritance model failed.
A selected parent looks exceptional but its offspring are highly variable and rarely reproduce the desired combination. The parent phenotype alone did not demonstrate strong transmitting value.
commonMistakes: Using genotype and phenotype as interchangeable terms.
Treating complex cultivation traits as simple dominant/recessive traits without evidence.
Ignoring environment when ranking related plants.
Drawing broad inheritance conclusions from very small populations.
Calling a trait stable after one generation.
Keeping records only for selected plants and losing information about the original population.
content.practicalApplication: Build a breeding observation record with parent IDs, cross direction, generation, population size, environment, predefined traits, measurement method, individual phenotype records, selection decisions and later progeny results. For a simulated family, identify which conclusions are directly supported by the observations and which would require more generations, more individuals or additional environments.
content.summary: Genetics connects inherited variation to observed traits through development and environment. Segregation and recombination create family variation; population size limits what can be observed; selection changes future generations; and progeny testing plus repeated evaluation are needed before making strong claims about transmission or stability.
